title: SMSF registration feedback sought
full_text:
The SMSF Association is seeking feedback from members on their experience with the fund registration process to identify what currently is and is not working well with this phase of these retirement savings vehicles.
The member consultation follows the government’s August policy announcements, which included the proposed expansion of ATO powers and compulsory education before a new SMSF is registered.
The association did not support “mandatory ‘one-size-fits-all’ education for all new SMSF trustees” at that time.
To assist members, the professional body has prepared a series of questions across five different areas to help them with their responses.
These questions cover numbers and timing, issues and contact, additional steps, declined registrations and other observations. The body is also asking for case studies members may have from real practice that may provide useful feedback.
“We are particularly interested in your experience with the timeliness of the SMSF registration process and cases where a client’s application may have run into difficulty,” the association stated in the consultation paper.
Questions to members concentrate on timeliness and include queries around how long registration typically takes from lodgement to confirmation and how many funds practitioners are registering.
Submissions are being sought from members who have assisted clients in registering a new SMSF with the ATO over the past 12 months. Members have until 13 November to make submissions and the association confirmed it may use anonymised feedback it receives in its submissions and ongoing advocacy.
“Member feedback is essential in helping us to identify issues and to inform and shape our ongoing advocacy in this area, and we encourage members to participate in this consultation,” it indicated.
The industry body also acknowledged positive feedback on smooth registrations was just as valuable as problem cases.
“This helps us better understand the current registration process and distinguish individual issues from more systemic ones,” it explained.
author: Jason Spits
